name: Yokukansan (Japanese Kampo herbal formula)
short: Pseudoaldosteronism from its licorice, which may cause death: case reports in older people of severe low potassium, torsade de pointes; low potassium in 8-24% in hospital studies; 2 lung-injury cases.
text: Yokukansan is a Japanese Kampo formula that contains licorice, and its best-documented serious harm is pseudoaldosteronism, which the authors of a Japanese adverse-drug-report study say leads to high blood pressure, low potassium and muscle weakness and may result in death; in that database of reported cases, yokukansan had a higher reporting odds ratio for pseudoaldosteronism than other licorice-containing Kampo formulas (2.4), which shows a reporting association, not how often it occurs. Case reports describe severe low potassium in an 81-year-old woman with dementia (1.29 mEq/l, with abnormal heart tracing) after 6 months of yokukansan, in an 88-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease (1.9 mmol/l, with metabolic alkalosis and respiratory acidosis), and in a 70-year-old woman who had also taken a second licorice-containing formula, Shakuyakukanzoto, until a month before admission (2.4 mmol/l); each improved after the herbal medicine was stopped and potassium was given. Another case report describes torsade de pointes, a dangerous heart-rhythm disturbance, with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy caused by licorice-induced pseudoaldosteronism in an older patient taking several medicines including yokukansan and galantamine; the abstract calls the arrhythmia fatal but does not say whether the patient survived. In hospital record studies, low potassium developed in 94 of 389 patients (24.2%) given yokukansan or a related licorice-containing formula (potassium below 3.6 mEq/L), in 53 of 304 psychiatric patients (17.4%) and in 55 of 665 patients (8.3%, potassium below 3.0 mEq/L); reported risk factors included older age, low blood albumin, full dosage and taking other potassium-lowering medicines (diuretics, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids or glycyrrhizin), and, in the 389-patient study, taking yokukansan itself rather than the related formula (hazard ratio 3.1). Two case reports describe drug-induced lung injury: pneumonitis in a 74-year-old man that improved with steroid pulse therapy, with a lymphocyte test positive for yokukansan, and lung injury in an 82-year-old woman taking yokukansan and another formula, Daisaikoto, with a basophil activation test positive for both. In trials, a 145-person placebo-controlled trial in Alzheimer's disease observed no serious adverse effects, and a meta-analysis of 5 trials (381 patients with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia) found no significant differences from controls in adverse events or discontinuations.
